implementation_notes: Ruby has Enumerator and Fiber, both continuations in different clothing. Enumerator#next resumes a suspended generator, returning each value in turn (the multi-shot form); Fiber is the general primitive - Fiber.yield suspends the whole call stack and returns control to the resumer, and Fiber#resume picks it back up, so a Fiber can suspend in the middle of a deep call chain. Fibers are asymmetric (they always return to their resumer), and since Ruby 3.x they are cheap enough for structured concurrency. There is no first-class continuation object, so CallCC-style general continuations are not available.
idiom_name: Enumerator (multi-shot generator continuation); Fiber (stackful asymmetric coroutine)
code_sketch:
def tree_each(node, &k)
  return if node.nil?
  tree_each(node.left, &k)
  k.call(node.value)
end

enum = Enumerator.new { |y| tree_each(root) { |v| y << v } }  # CPS by block

fiber = Fiber.new do
  a = Fiber.yield 1            # suspends the whole stack, returns to the resumer
  Fiber.yield a + 1            # resumed here
end
fiber.resume                   # => 1
fiber.resume(10)               # => 11
pitfalls: A block converted with &block then called with .call has proc semantics (no arity check); lambda has stricter arity checking - mixing them changes which return you wrote.
A Fiber that is never resumed keeps everything it captured alive, and an abandoned fiber inside a loop leaks one frame set per iteration.
An Enumerator that is not exhausted and not explicitly closed keeps its suspended frame - the generator's GC problem in Ruby form.
